newsitem.title: UK: Bruton hopes for historic N. Ireland breakthrough.
newsitem.headline: Bruton hopes for historic N. Ireland breakthrough.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said on Wednesday that prospects for peace in Northern Ireland were better than they ever had been following Labour's election landslide, provided the IRA declares a ceasefire.
"We're reaching a point where the difficulties which have bedevilled us in Anglo-Irish relationships for generations can be resolved," he told reporters before giving a speech to the Oxford Union.
"There never has been and perhaps never will be as good an opportunity as we have today. The only ingredient missing is an IRA ceasefire," he said.
The Irish Republican Army, which has fought for more than 25 years to oust Britain from Northern Ireland, ended a 17- month ceasefire in February 1996.
In his speech, Bruton said a detailed plan for peace was already in place.
The first element consisted of peace talks open to all political parties and involving both the British and Irish governments, and the second was an end to IRA violence.

"The republican movement should make up its mind, once and for all, unreservedly to enter the political process, and throw away for good the crutch of violence or threatened violence. Once it does that, the road to peace and prosperity is open to all," Bruton said.

Bruton was to meet Britain's new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair on Thursday. Political analysts hoped Blair's landslide election victory would enable him to make better progress towards a lasting peace in the British-ruled province.
"There is a determination in this government to resolve issues that governments in the last 20 or 30 years have not been able to resolve," Bruton told reporters.
"This new government has a strong mandate and a leadership capable of making very important decisions very quickly."
Bruton outlined achievements of the peace talks that opened in Belfast nearly a year ago, and which will resume on June 3.

The IRA, which has fought for more than 25 years to oust Britain from Northern Ireland, ended its 17-month ceasefire in 1996 accusing then-prime minister John Major of intransigence and striking deals with the pro-British Ulster Unionists to stay in power.
With a 179-seat majority in the new parliament, Blair will not face a similar stranglehold but he has insisted the IRA call a new truce before entering all-party talks.

"If they (the Republican movement) make good their promise to take the political road, the two governments will receive them...into inclusive talks where no topic is excluded and all the relevant players are present," Bruton promised.
